NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION) — The question-answered sentence first: A membrane hydration maintenance system using electroosmotic pumping within the membrane structure to redistribute water from the anode to the cathode during high current density operation. Standard practice: Increases cathode humidification (increased parasitic load). Your mitigation: Electroosmotic pumping leverages the proton transport mechanism to actively move water molecules against concentration gradients without external energy input. Adjacent-technique clearance: Closest existing practice is external humidification systems; yours differs by operating internally within the membrane structure using existing proton transport physics. The intervention attacks the failure by maintaining membrane hydration at the cathode side where dehydration occurs during high current density operation.

PHYSICS CHECK — The governing physical relation is the electroosmotic flux equation: J_eo = -n·μ·E·C, where n is the number of water molecules per proton, μ is electroosmotic mobility, E is electric field, and C is water concentration. During high current density, the electric field across the membrane increases, enhancing electroosmotic water transport from anode to cathode. Magnitude verification: At 1.5 A/cm², the proton flux is ~15.5 mA/cm², potentially moving ~0.3 μL/cm²/min of water, sufficient to offset dehydration rates of ~0.2 μL/cm²/min observed in standard practice.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL — Standard practice components: Cathode humidifier system, water injection pump, humidity sensor. Your intervention components:
- Electroosmotic enhancement layer (b) - Standard catalyst-coated membrane (CCM) with modified ionomer containing hydrophilic additives
- Anode-side water retention grid (a) - Utilizes existing anode flow field material with modified surface properties
- Membrane electrode assembly (MEA) reconfiguration procedure (c) - Assembly process optimized for enhanced water transport properties
- Operating parameter adjustment (c) - Anode/cathode stoichiometry ratio adjusted to 1.2/1.5 to optimize water availability

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY) — Standard practice: Cathode humidifier system (added parasitic load), water injection pump (energy consumption), humidity sensor (monitoring). Your intervention: Electroosmotic enhancement layer (material substitution within existing CCM class), anode-side water retention grid (modification of existing flow field), MEA reconfiguration procedure (existing assembly process adjustment), operating parameter adjustment (software change). Burden conclusion: Same burden class - all changes utilize existing manufacturing infrastructure and require no additional hardware beyond standard fuel cell components.

EXECUTABLE TEST — Protocol: Operate fuel cell stack at 1.5 A/cm² and 80°C for 500 hours with anode/cathode stoichiometry ratio of 1.2/1.5. Instruments: In-situ membrane resistance measurement system, temperature mapping sensors, water balance meters. Pass/fail threshold: Stack power degradation <10% over test period, no localized hot spots (>5°C above average), membrane resistance increase <20%. Duration: 500 hours continuous operation. Kill criterion: Any single measurement exceeds pass/fail threshold at any point during testing.
